title: Which number in the box looks special?
description: Four numbers sit in a box, and each one has a feature that the other three do not share. The video finds a reason for every number, and Keeko's doubt that only one number can be special is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number can stand out for its digits, its multiples, its squares or its divisors, and each of the four numbers has its own reason. Watch for students who think there is one right answer.

source: There are four numbers in this box (9, 16, 25, 43). Which number looks special to you? Why do you say so?
video_script.why: The child looks at the four numbers by their digits, their multiples, their squares and their divisors, and finds a reason for each number to stand out.
video_script.substitution: Compare the four numbers by digits, by multiples, by squares and by what divides them, and look for a feature that only one number has.
video_script.anchor: a box holding four number cards: 9, 16, 25 and 43
video_script.wrong_answer: only one of the four numbers can be special
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says only one of the four numbers can be special, because the question asks which number looks special. Nine is the only multiple of three, sixteen is the only even number, twenty five is the only multiple of five and forty three is the only prime, so the bubble is struck through.
video_script.payoff_line: Each of the four numbers is special for its own reason

final_answer.value: Any of them can be special: 9 is the only multiple of 3, 16 is the only multiple of 4, 25 is the only multiple of 5, 43 is the only prime
final_answer.spoken: any of them can be special, nine is the only multiple of three, sixteen is the only multiple of four, twenty five is the only multiple of five, and forty three is the only prime

hold_back: Answer: Any of them can be special: 9 is the only multiple of 3, 16 is the only multiple of 4, 25 is the only multiple of 5, 43 is the only prime
maths_rules: 9 is the only single-digit number; 16 is the only even number
9 = 3 x 3, and 16 = 5 x 3 + 1, 25 = 8 x 3 + 1, 43 = 14 x 3 + 1 leave 1 over, so 9 is the only multiple of 3
16 = 4 x 4, and 9, 25 and 43 are odd, so 16 is the only multiple of 4
25 = 5 x 5, and 9, 16 and 43 do not end in 0 or 5, so 25 is the only multiple of 5
9 = 3 x 3, 16 = 4 x 4 and 25 = 5 x 5 are squares; 43 lies between 36 = 6 x 6 and 49 = 7 x 7, so it is the only number that is not a square
43 = 2 x 21 + 1 = 3 x 14 + 1 = 4 x 10 + 3 = 5 x 8 + 3 = 6 x 7 + 1; no number from 2 to 42 divides 43, so 43 is the only prime
video_script.design: One idea: a number can stand out in several ways, and every number in the box has its own reason. Assumes multiples and squares. Wrong idea: only one number can be special. The box of four cards stays on the board to the end.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks only one of the four numbers can be special.
<bookmark mark='why'/>The reason is that the question asks which number looks special.
<bookmark mark='each'/>But we found a reason for every card. Nine has one digit, and sixteen is even.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>Twenty five is the only multiple of five, and forty three is a prime.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Different people can pick different numbers, and each one can be right.
